title: Heterogeneous Element-Aware Cross-Version Differencing of Scientific Documents via Layout-Aware Alignment and Structure-Aware Reasoning
research_question: How can two revised scientific PDF versions be aligned and differenced at the element level while preserving layout and internal structure across text, tables, formulas, and figures?
methodology: The framework first parses each document into typed heterogeneous elements with page-layout coordinates and type-specific representations for text, tables, formulas, and figures. It then performs same-type cross-version alignment using a candidate page window, similarity retrieval, and weighted location, content, and structural signals, treating unmatched elements as insertions or deletions. A structure-aware reasoning stage characterizes localized content, formatting, and structural differences. The system is evaluated on scientific-document version pairs drawn from real journal-production proofreading workflows, using detection, localization, structural-consistency, alignment, and matching metrics.

key_findings.finding: The proposed method achieved detection F1 scores of 0.903 for text, 0.855 for tables, 0.862 for formulas, and 0.845 for figures on the evaluation corpus.

Cross-version alignment was a critical component: removing it reduced detection F1 from 0.866 to 0.779, localization F1 from 0.833 to 0.706, alignment accuracy from 0.856 to 0.681, and matching F1 from 0.859 to 0.692.
Type-specific alignment weights outperformed uniform shared weights, supporting the use of different mixtures of spatial, content, and structural evidence for heterogeneous element types.
Structural modeling produced particularly large gains for table-topology and formula-hierarchy changes, while content signals were comparatively more important for text and figures.
A soft candidate window of plus or minus two pages produced the strongest reported overall alignment results, outperforming same-page-only matching and a wider plus or minus three-page window.
The method supports element-level lineage across document revisions by explicitly matching corresponding typed elements before reasoning about content, formatting, and structural changes.

limitations: The alignment formulation primarily assumes one-to-one element correspondence and is less suitable for paragraph splits or merges, multi-page table decomposition, and major document restructuring.
Errors in upstream layout parsing, table-cell reconstruction, formula recognition, or figure extraction can propagate into alignment and differencing.
Figure comparison is mainly region-level because large-scale component-level structural annotations are unavailable.
The evaluation is concentrated on scientific PDFs from production proofreading workflows, so broader generalization to other document genres remains unverified.
raw_claims: The system decomposes each document version into typed elements with explicit page-layout coordinates.
Text, tables, formulas, and figures receive different structured representations.
Cross-version candidates are restricted to matching semantic element types.
Alignment combines spatial position, content similarity, and structural similarity with type-specific weights.
Unmatched elements are interpreted as insertions or deletions.
The evaluation corpus originates from real scientific-publishing proofreading workflows involving successive document versions.
Cross-version alignment contributes substantially to final detection and localization quality.
Tables and formulas benefit strongly from structure-aware comparison.
A two-page alignment window balances robustness to pagination shifts against spurious candidates.
The current one-to-one alignment model does not fully represent split, merged, or extensively reorganized elements.
